title: What's the Simplest Thing That Could Actually Work Here?
summary: Tests whether you default to starting simple and adding complexity only when justified — a proactive design stance, distinct from spotting over-engineering after the fact in an existing design.

slides.markdown:
The interviewer asks: **"what's the simplest thing that could actually work here?"** Leading with the simple answer signals more seniority than leading with the impressive one — it shows you calibrate complexity to the actual requirements instead of reaching for the most sophisticated tool you know.

This is the proactive counterpart to spotting over-engineering: instead of critiquing an existing design, you're choosing not to over-build one in the first place.

Ask what the actual current scale and realistic near-term scale are — as opposed to the scale the problem statement's *name* makes you imagine. "Design a URL shortener" sounds like it should handle billions of requests; the interviewer's actual stated numbers might be a small internal tool.

Anchoring to the name instead of the stated numbers is one of the most common ways candidates talk themselves into unnecessary complexity before they've even started designing.

State the simplest architecture that meets the actual stated requirements first, explicitly, before layering in complexity. Add each piece of complexity only tied to a specific requirement it solves.

The word "explicitly" matters — say the simple version out loud as your starting point, rather than silently designing the complex version and never mentioning the simpler alternative existed.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: the URL shortener's simplest version
slides.markdown:
Asked to "design a URL shortener," the simplest thing that could work is a single service with a relational database and a base62-encoded auto-increment ID — no distributed ID generation, no sharding, no CDN. State this plainly as the starting point before discussing what changes at scale.

This sounds almost too simple to say out loud in an interview, which is exactly why saying it explicitly is the signal — it shows you're not reaching for complexity out of habit or nerves.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: jumping straight to the complex end state
slides.markdown:
A concrete scenario: a candidate jumps straight to a multi-region, sharded, cache-everywhere design for a problem whose stated scale is 10,000 users. The interviewer has to redirect them back to something reasonable for the actual numbers given, costing the candidate time and signaling they don't calibrate complexity to requirements.

The redirect itself is a bad sign in an interview — it means the interviewer spent time steering you back instead of watching you drive the design forward on your own judgment.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: using the simple starting point in the room
slides.markdown:
![Escalation path from a simple single-DB start to adding Y once it breaks at X](assets/escalation-path.svg)

State the simple version, then proactively walk forward: "this works fine until X, at which point I'd add Y" — showing the escalation path rather than skipping straight to the complex end state.

This is the concrete technique for making "start simple" read as calibration rather than as not knowing the advanced material — you narrate the whole path, you just don't build past the point the requirements actually call for.

assets.alt: Escalation path from a simple single-DB start to adding Y once it breaks at X

slides.sectionTitle: The trade-off to name out loud
slides.markdown:
Starting simple risks looking like you don't know the advanced techniques if you never get to layer them in. The fix is stating the simple answer *and* immediately naming what would break it and what you'd add — so the simplicity reads as calibration, not as a knowledge gap.

This is why the escalation path (previous slide) matters so much: without it, "start simple" and "don't know better" are indistinguishable to the interviewer. With it, they're clearly different.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: would you really ship without a cache or CDN?
slides.markdown:
Follow-up: "so you'd really ship this without a cache or a CDN at all?" Yes, if the stated scale doesn't need one yet. Naming the exact metric that would trigger adding one is a stronger answer than adding it preemptively "to be safe."

A concrete trigger — "once read latency from origin crosses 200ms at p99, I'd add a CDN" — shows the omission was a deliberate, checkable decision, not an oversight.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: the risk of starting simple if you're wrong about scale
slides.markdown:
Follow-up: "what's the risk of starting simple if you're wrong about the scale?" Name the migration cost of adding the complexity later versus the cost of carrying it unused now — for most components, adding it later is cheaper than most candidates assume, which is the actual argument for starting simple.

This reframes the perceived risk: candidates often overestimate how expensive it is to add a cache or a CDN after the fact, and underestimate how expensive it is to carry unused complexity from day one.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: opening with the most sophisticated architecture
slides.markdown:
**Wrong move:** opening with the most sophisticated architecture you know, regardless of the stated scale, because it feels like it demonstrates more knowledge.

**Why it's wrong:** it signals you don't calibrate complexity to actual requirements, and it often forces the interviewer to redirect you back to something reasonable — a costly correction that eats into your time and reads worse than starting simple ever would have.

**Correct model:** state the simple version first, then demonstrate the same knowledge by narrating the escalation path forward from it.

State the simplest architecture that meets the actual stated scale first, explicitly. Then narrate the escalation path forward — "this works until X, at which point I'd add Y" — so the simplicity reads as calibration, not as a gap in knowledge.

When pushed on a specific omission (no cache, no CDN), name the exact metric that would trigger adding it. When pushed on the risk of being wrong about scale, name that adding complexity later is usually cheaper than carrying it unused from day one.
